name: Content first
summary: Large, calm type and generous space, for people who come to read.
description: Content first is an Open DS scheme: a full set of answers to the Open DS grammar, with the reasons behind each, usage rules, voice and tone, and the tokens that follow. Large, calm type and generous space, for people who come to read.

ai.use_when: Publications, documentation, blogs, guides and help centers.
ai.avoid_when: Data-heavy tools or screens with many actions.

scenarios.text: A reader arrives from search on a phone and reads a long guide in one sitting.
A returning reader saves an article to finish on the train.

summary.text: Conversational and warm. Talk to one reader, like a good editor would.

principles.text: Short sentences with room to breathe.
Explain why before asking for anything.
A button label stays on one line: it never breaks onto two.

out.why: Readers need sections, navigation and little else. Files attach to messages, and Content first carries no conversations: people read from start to end.
Readers need sections, navigation and little else. Bubbles are for back-and-forth chat, and the catalogue rules them out for long text.
Content first keeps one clear action per section, and alternatives are text links so they do not compete. Joined buttons work against that.
Readers need sections, navigation and little else. Actions are rare: subscribe, share, save. Picking dates is not one of them.
Readers need sections, navigation and little else. Actions are rare: subscribe, share, save. The catalogue rules combobox out for searching a whole site; search is a plain input.
Command suits expert users who type to jump anywhere. Most readers visit now and then, and the catalogue rules it out for them.
Right-click menus suit power users. Readers are occasional visitors who see the interface fresh each time, and arrive on phones too.
Content first avoids data-heavy tools. It has no dense tables, and its rows are read, not scanned.
Readers need sections, navigation and little else. Actions are rare: subscribe, share, save. Picking a date or range is not one of them.
Content first keeps few components, covered by today's pages. Sheet already holds the phone menu, and forms are rare and short.
Readers arrive on phones and laptops alike, and touch screens have no hover. Occasional visitors need visible words, not hidden previews.
Forms are rare and short: newsletter and search. Actions are rare: subscribe, share, save. No step asks for a one-time code.
Most readers visit now and then and see the interface fresh each time. Shortcuts serve repeat experts, and command is left out too.
Readers need sections, navigation and little else. Markers split conversations, and Content first separates sections with space, not lines.
Menubar is for dense desktop-style tools, not website navigation or phones. Content first avoids screens with many actions, and readers arrive on phones.
Readers need sections, navigation and little else. People read from start to end; actions are rare: subscribe, share, save. No comments or feeds are among them.
Readers need sections, navigation and little else. It keeps live chat in view, and people here read from start to end.
Only menus and dialogs float in Content first. A long aside opens in place with collapsible instead.
Forms are rare and short, so there are no steps to count. Skeleton already holds article text while it loads.
Resizable panels are for desktop tools, not phones. Content first readers arrive on phones and laptops alike, and it avoids data-heavy tools.
Sidebar is app navigation, not a website's main navigation. Content first is a public site; navigation menu carries the site sections and sheet the phone menu.
Readers need sections, navigation and little else. Actions are rare: subscribe, share, save. Dragging a value is not one of them.
Forms are rare and short: newsletter and search, both one line. Actions are rare: subscribe, share, save. None calls for long text entry.
Readers need sections, navigation and little else. Toggles format text in a toolbar, and Content first avoids screens with many actions.
Readers need sections, navigation and little else. Actions are rare: subscribe, share, save. Switching views between modes is not one of them.
Readers arrive on any device, and on touch screens hover hints never show. Icons always carry a visible word instead.

answers.question: brand.q3
answers.why: Source Serif 4 for reading and headings, Inter for labels and captions: a good magazine's text with a quiet interface.

considers.readability: Source Serif 4 is a reading serif made for long text; its optical sizes keep body text open and even.
considers.legibility: Labels and captions sit in Inter, a sans with a tall x-height that stays clear at small sizes.
considers.scalability: Source Serif 4's optical sizes adjust the design from caption to display, so one family spans the scale.
considers.numerals: Data is rare here; numbers sit in the reading serif, set in running text rather than tables.
considers.scripts: Both cover Latin, Cyrillic and Greek; Hebrew and Arabic need another face, chosen to match.
considers.recognition: The brand shows in type, not in color, so the serif is the brand.
considers.familiarity: Serif text reads like a book or an article, which long-form readers know.
considers.personality: Warm and considered, as the brand answer asks.
considers.performance: Two variable families, one file each.
considers.licensing: SIL Open Font License, both: free to embed in apps and on the web.
considers.fallback: Falls back to Georgia and system-ui, as its tokens say; Inter is the serif's interface pair.

color.$description: Color options: raw hue ramps. Each hue has a light ramp and a dark ramp (the same steps tuned for dark backgrounds). Steps only: each theme decides its own base (@). Themes pick from these; components never read them.

stone.$description: The stone hue: a light ramp, a dark ramp and its base value.

150.$description: Derived: the step between 100 and 200 on the scheme's step curve (light-ease), even in contrast. Added so a floating layer sits one step above raised in dark.

400.$description: Derived: the OKLab midpoint of 300 and 500. Added so muted text can pass 4.5:1 and stay quieter than secondary.

600.$description: Derived: the OKLab midpoint of 500 and 700. Added so muted text can pass 4.5:1 and stay quieter than secondary.

150.$description: Derived: the step between 100 and 200 on the scheme's step curve (light-ease), even in contrast. Added so a floating layer sits one step above raised in dark. Moved 0.025 darker in OKLab lightness, so muted text keeps its 4.5:1 floor on a floating layer, with a 0.1 margin.

400.$description: Derived: the OKLab midpoint of 300 and 500. Added so muted text can pass 4.5:1 and stay quieter than secondary.

600.$description: Derived: the OKLab midpoint of 500 and 700. Added so muted text can pass 4.5:1 and stay quieter than secondary.

floor.$description: Derived: step 0 at 0.04 lower OKLab lightness, its hue and chroma kept. Added so a dark well sits below a canvas on 0.

navy.$description: The navy hue: a light ramp, a dark ramp and its base value.

green.$description: The green hue: a light ramp, a dark ramp and its base value.

100.why: This step is the soft background of status messages in light mode and the status text in dark mode. As generated, the text looked white on dark backgrounds, so the step got a little more color, and blue and red a touch darker, until the color showed.

space.$description: Space options. Names give the size in pixels at the default text size; values are rem.

size.$description: Size options for controls, rows and icons.

round.$description: A circle of a square: avatars, radio dots, thumbs and round buttons.

pill.$description: A capsule of any box: tracks, progress, the scroll thumb and pill controls.

size.$description: Type size options. Names are pixels at the default text size; values are rem, so text grows with the user's setting.

line-height.$description: Line height options: ratios of the text size. The type scale generates them.

family.$description: Font family options. Each brand's theme picks its display, body, interface and data fonts from these.

moderate.$description: Moderate: a calm, easy-to-follow speed, about 150ms.

relaxed.$description: Relaxed: a slower speed for larger moves, about 300ms.

standard.$description: A standard ease-out: fast at the start, settling slowly, with no overshoot.

strong-out.$description: A strong ease-out: most of the way in the first third of the time, then a soft stop. For exits.

shadow.$description: Raw shadows. Elevation semantics point at these.

overlay.$description: Raw shadow for overlay in light mode.

overlay-dark.$description: Raw shadow for overlay in dark mode.

1_5.$description: An icon stroke width option, on Lucide's 24px grid.

open-ds.why: A touch target sets the 48px default. Compact is one 4px step below it, 44px, the touch-size hit area itself; large equals the default, as actions are rare and calm. The scheme has no row role, so a row takes the default.
Spacious: room around the text helps reading, so panels and fields breathe; rows stay tight.
